profiles.meeting_scenario: At a hospital radiation oncology department, a breast radiation oncologist and the lead medical physicist meet to plan the clinical rollout of a semi-automatic Pinnacle3 tangential IMRT technique for whole-breast irradiation, using recent left-sided free-breathing, left-sided DIBH, and right-sided cases as the practical reference. The agenda is to decide which patients will be included in the initial rollout, what historical 3DCRT plans will be used as the comparison set, how much staffing time the new workflow is expected to save, and what safety/robustness checks will be done before routine use. The expected outcome is a shared rollout plan for a small pilot, with responsibilities and a target date for presenting the technique at the department breast QA meeting.

members.name: Dr. Sofia Lindberg
members.role: Consultant Radiation Oncologist, Breast Service Lead
members.expertise: Breast radiotherapy, contour review, clinical plan approval, DIBH workflow
members.background: Sofia has led the breast site group for four years and signs off most whole-breast plans; she is clinically focused and used to thinking in terms of review-ready plans, treatment slots, and edge-case anatomy that still fits standard tangents.
members.private_state: She wants to reduce planning delays without increasing the amount of physician rework, and she wants the new technique to be broad enough that the breast team can actually use it in routine clinic rather than only for a narrow subset.
hidden_assumptions: "Whole-breast cases" includes nearly all standard tangential breast-only patients, even if they have minor contour irregularities, visible seroma clips, or slightly customized field edges that still feel routine to the breast team.
"Clinical plan" means the physician-approved plan that was ultimately used for treatment decisions, including any late manual shaping or small dosimetrist edits made before treatment start.
"Planning time" means the practical elapsed effort needed to get to a physician-reviewable plan in the daily clinic workflow, not just the minutes of direct TPS interaction.
"First-week check" means reviewing actual early patient plans and images in the normal clinical pathway to make sure the technique behaves safely in practice.
If a technique is said to be robust with respect to shifts, that robustness should still be visible in the first treated patients, not only in commissioning-style test cases.

members.name: Erik Nyström
members.role: Senior Medical Physicist and TPS Automation Lead
members.expertise: Treatment planning system configuration, Pinnacle3 Auto-Planning, commissioning, dosimetric benchmarking
members.background: Erik built the auto-planning template and has been comparing generated tangential IMRT plans against archived 3DCRT plans; he is process-oriented and thinks in terms of template scope, reproducibility, and measurable hands-on workload reduction.
members.private_state: He wants a tightly controlled rollout that shows clear efficiency gains and avoids creating extra ad hoc review work for the physics team, while keeping the first implementation limited to cases that match the commissioning assumptions.
hidden_assumptions: "Whole-breast cases" means uncomplicated breast-only tangential cases that match the template design boundary: no nodal targets, no implants, no unusual target cropping, and no expected manual beam customization beyond routine setup.

"Clinical plan" means the archived reference 3DCRT plan stored in Pinnacle for dosimetric comparison, typically the plan at approval/export stage rather than every later workflow modification outside the benchmark dataset.
"Planning time" means active planner hands-on time to generate and tune the plan within Pinnacle, because that is the relevant quantity for demonstrating automation benefit.

"First-week check" can be satisfied by a predefined robustness exercise on representative early cases, such as applying virtual 5 mm isocenter shifts, without adding patient-by-patient operational oversight.
Once the template has passed commissioning and benchmark comparison, routine clinical use should not require a separate special review layer beyond standard physics checks.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the pilot will cover "whole-breast" or "standard tangential" patients.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means most breast-only tangent patients seen in routine clinic, including mildly irregular but still familiar cases such as seroma-clip guidance, slightly extended inferior folds, or physician-customized tangent edges that are still considered standard by the breast service.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means only clean template-matching breast-only tangent cases with no expected manual beam reshaping and no anatomy or contour features likely to push the auto-technique outside its commissioned envelope.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using common departmental shorthand for a familiar category, and the borderline cases feel too routine to Sofia and too obviously out-of-scope to Erik for either of them to think the category itself needs unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the 'clinical 3DCRT plan' for comparison
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to compare autoIMRT against the "clinical plans" from recent breast patients.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the final physician-approved treatment plans as they were effectively used in patient care, including the last small shaping adjustments that made the plans clinically acceptable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the archived Pinnacle benchmark plans he can systematically extract, which may correspond to the stored approved/exported 3DCRT objects rather than every later practical adjustment or alternate plan version remembered by clinicians.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The department routinely refers to prior treated plans simply as "the clinical plans," and both assume there is only one obvious version per patient even though different workflow artifacts can legitimately feel like the same plan.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both use the phrase "planning time" when discussing expected efficiency gains.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means end-to-end time until a review-ready plan reaches the physician in normal workflow, including setup, auto-run, any required cleanup, and the delay before she can actually review it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the dosimetrist or physicist's active hands-on time inside the TPS to launch the template and make minimal interactions, which is the six-minute figure he associates with autoIMRT.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standardized because time-saving is an accepted benefit of automation, and neither realizes the other is using a different operational definition of the same headline number.

misalignment_points.topic: What the 'first-week robustness check' consists of
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree there should be a "first-week check" or "robustness check" before broader rollout.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means reviewing the first treated patients in the live clinical pathway, with attention to whether the plans and image-guidance look acceptable in real use before the pathway is expanded.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means running the predefined commissioning-style robustness method on early cases, specifically virtual isocenter shifts such as plus/minus 5 mm, after which standard workflow is sufficient.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see the check as a sensible safety step and use the same reassuring label, but each silently maps it onto the checking mechanism most natural in their own role: clinical early-case oversight versus physics-style robustness testing.

I do not want a pilot that only works for the easiest handful and then creates more physician rework later.
